Mary Morgan was handed a £378,000 payment "under contractual redundancy terms" when she retired from a senior role in Scotland's NHS earlier this year

An NHS executive has received a near £400,000 redundancy pay-off after retiring from a health board, new figures show.

Following a 44-year career in the health service, Mary Morgan retired as chief executive of NHS National Services Scotland (NSS) in May.

But it has now been revealed Morgan received a £378,000 payment "under contractual redundancy terms" as part of an exit that came after NHS NSS was merged into a new quango called Public Services Delivery (PSD) Scotland in April.

A PSD Scotland spokesperson said Morgan retired after an "exceptional career" and all payments were in accordance with the terms and conditions of her employment.

The payment comes ahead of a planned major overhaul of Scotland's NHS which could see the number of health boards cut dramatically.

Swinney to cut number of health boards from 14 to two

Doctors say radical plan to merge Scotland's health boards should be scrapped

PSD Scotland started operating in in April , external and was set up to drive changes across the health and care system, and the wider public sector.

It replaced both NHS NSS and another quango called NHS Education for Scotland, whose chief executive Prof Karen Reid is now in charge of PSD Scotland.

Morgan, who earned between £160,000 and £165,000 a year, had been chief executive of NHS NSS since 2021.

BBC Scotland asked NHS NSS on 10 March what would happen with Morgan now her role was defunct.

The health board said the senior NHS executive was "considering her options and next opportunity in line with national workforce policies".

After a follow-up query three weeks later, Keith Redpath, the then chairman of NHS NSS, replied: "Mary Morgan retires on 3 May, concluding an exceptional 44-year career in NHS Scotland."

The NHS NSS accounts for 2025/26 , external show Morgan retired under contractual redundancy terms from PSD Scotland on 3 May and received a related amount of £378,000.

The same accounts show Morgan's pension pot, known as The Cash Equivalent Transfer Value, is just over £2m.

A PSD Scotland spokesperson said: "Mary Morgan retired on 3 May, concluding an exceptional 44-year career in NHS Scotland. All payment received was in accordance to the terms and conditions of her employment."

The BBC has approached Morgan, but she declined to comment.

MN202611_x6qu95jqpz.t:
"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang

US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.

A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

Michael Carrick arrived at Manchester United's training ground on Tuesday

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick's future will be decided at a meeting on Wednesday attended by owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who remains supportive of executives Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox.

Carrick's position is under threat after the club slipped to 18th in the Premier League following a chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Minority owner Ratcliffe, chief executive Berrada and director of football Wilcox will meet in Monaco to decide the 45-year-old's future.

BBC Sport reported on Monday there was a growing expectation Berrada and Wilcox would recommend to Ratcliffe and majority owners, the Glazer family, that Carrick be sacked.

They will present their recommendation, although the Glazers will also be consulted, and a decision on the manager's future may not be announced until Thursday.

BBC Sport also understands at this stage Ratcliffe remains supportive of Berrada and Wilcox, despite mounting criticism of the pair from fans.

Berrada and Wilcox recommended Carrick be appointed permanent head coach in May after an impressive spell as interim boss.

Wednesday's meeting in Monaco, which is where Ratcliffe is based, was already planned and has not been organised to strictly discuss Carrick's future.

However, that will form part of the talks, which could also include whether to bolster his coaching team.

If the decision to sack Carrick is made at the meeting, the club want to inform him face to face. He is said to understand that United's form has made discussions over his future inevitable.

United have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years, but the hierarchy still believe a top-five finish is possible.

The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd

How close is Carrick to Man United exit?

BBC Sport reported in October United had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann about replacing Carrick.

Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford.

Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August.

However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.

Man Utd score twice in stoppage-time to share points in eight-goal thriller

Pochettino, Howe, Emery... or Carrick? Man Utd's managerial options

The draw with Villa was Carrick's third match in charge since the club opted to give the 45-year-old more time at Old Trafford.

Results during that time - a win, a draw and a defeat - were mixed, and displayed the best and worst of Carrick's reign with United shipping goals but displaying good character to come back from two goals down on three occasions.

United's board toyed with sacking Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth, but decided the Englishman - and his players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around.

It was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.

Unfortunately for Carrick, it makes for poor reading.

With one victory in 10 Premier League matches, United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986-87 season.

They sit 18th in the table, one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace.

Only the Eagles and Ipswich have conceded more than the 19 goals United have shipped in the Premier League this season.

It is hard to believe given the club's current predicament just how quickly Carrick's tenure has soured.

Four 'huge mistakes' that show Man Utd's defensive problems

Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser.

The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.

After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton.

Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.

Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.

The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.

By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.

After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.

He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.

With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.

"It's a miracle that I'm still here," says Danny Ellis

What seemed like a simple case of toothache led to a rare heart condition, sepsis and doctors believing Danny Ellis had just a 1% chance of survival.

The 42-year-old from Llanrwst in Conwy county began experiencing tooth pain in April, and went to the dentist where he was given antibiotics.

But the pain kept returning and it was not until he was left with red marks on his body that he was finally rushed to hospital.

Doctors told him it was a "miracle" he was still alive after an initial heart operation failed, and he suffered a series of strokes - but he pulled through against the odds.

The recovery process will continue for at least another 12 months, Danny said, and he will likely be on medication for the rest of his life, but little milestones are getting him through.

"At the moment, I'm able to take my daughter to school, and that's enough for now," he said.

"I still feel different on my left side, and I can easily get tired and forget what I'm supposed to say at times, but I hope that will improve with time."

Danny says the support of his wife Ceri and his daughter Harriet has got him through

Danny said after the toothache got worse, an X-ray at his dentist in Colwyn Bay showed no signs of infection, and he returned home with another course of antibiotics.

A pattern which saw the pain ease and return continued for several weeks and Danny noticed he was losing his strength and red marks were appearing on his body.

"The pain was terrible and I had to take a week off work, something I would never do," said Danny, who runs the Spar shop in Betws-y-Coed, as well as Gwalia bakery in Pwllheli, Gwynedd.

"The symptoms were starting to get worse, and the pain too, especially in my legs. I didn't know what was going on."

By Father's Day on 21 June, Danny was feeling "out of it" and "unable to remember what I'd received as presents".

When his wife Ceri arrived home from work, she found him lying on the couch with bruises on his body.

Danny credits his wife, Ceri, with saving his life

They went to the GP surgery in Betws-y-Coed on 23 June and, after several tests, Danny was rushed by ambulance to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

"I remember seeing the nurse run out of the room to call for an ambulance," Danny said.

When he told doctors at the hospital that he had a toothache and had been on antibiotics, their "face immediately changed" and they ordered an echocardiogram , external - which scans the heart.

The scan found a hole in the mitral valve in Danny's heart, and it was also discovered he had developed sepsis , external and there was fluid in his lungs.

Sepsis is a serious, life-threatening reaction to an infection and can develop very quickly.

"The marks on my hands had turned from red to black - the sepsis was killing me," he said.

"The doctor said at the time that I was lucky to be alive but I was fighting for life."

Danny said he was diagnosed with endocarditis , external , a rare inflammation of the inner lining of the heart which is usually caused by an infection.

According to the NHS, endocarditis usually happens when bacteria or fungus gets into the blood through the mouth or skin and travels to the heart - which was why Danny's pain initially appeared to be a toothache.

It says the most common symptoms are a high temperature, headache, feeling very tired, joint or muscle pain, night sweats, feeling breathless, loss of appetite, or losing weight without trying.

"The marks on my hands had turned from red to black - the sepsis was killing me," says Danny

"They wanted to transfer me to Broadgreen Hospital in Liverpool but I wouldn't have survived the journey," said Danny.

He had to stay in hospital in Bangor until he was "strong enough" to make the trip, and underwent heart surgery in Liverpool on 6 July, which lasted six hours.

"My brother told me after that the operation was unsuccessful," he said.

"That was the first time the situation hit me on an emotional level and I felt really sad. I told my brother that I was tired of the whole thing, tired of fighting."

But, within a couple of days, a doctor told Danny that they had been given a special machine to help his blood clot properly, and they wanted to try the operation again.

It was successful the second time, with the infection cleared and the hole in the mitral valve closed.

After the operation, Danny was told he had suffered a series of strokes while in and out of consciousness.

"When the doctor was reading his notes afterwards, he said it was a miracle that I was still alive," said Danny, adding he had been told "the probability of survival was 1%".

Danny was transferred back to Ysbyty Gwynedd to begin his recovery.

"I couldn't walk at first, I didn't have the strength to do anything," he said.

But Danny said he saw progress after a couple of weeks, adding: "I walked with my daughter, Harriet, for the first time in months and that was very emotional.

"My family were a big part of my recovery and a big help as I fought through the whole thing. That's what got me through."

Danny says walking with his daughter for the first time after his surgery was "very emotional"

Danny was released from hospital on 19 August and says one of the first things he did was visit his dentist "because I knew he was very emotional about the situation".

"It wasn't his fault at all, my case and how it developed was something so rare," he said.

"I look after my teeth, clean them twice a day, so there's nothing I could have done differently. It's still a mystery to tell the truth.

"I had the worst possible scenario in my experience. Anyone can have toothache but, when endocarditis is part of it, that's when things change."

Danny said he was "extremely grateful" for all the support he had received in recent months.

"All the staff at Liverpool, Bangor - they've been amazing," he said.

"I'm meeting the surgeon from Broadgreen for the first time since the operation - that will be very emotional."

He added: "But Ceri made the first call, she was worried at first. If I had waited another day or two, the story would have been very different.

Brady brought an end to his illustrious NFL career in 2023

NFL legend Tom Brady has ended his association with top-of-the-table Championship side Birmingham City.

The record seven-time Super Bowl champion became a minority owner in the St Andrew's club in August 2023 when he "entered a partnership" with club owners Knighthead Capital Management LLC.

Part of Brady's role involved him being chairman of an advisory board at Birmingham, with the club saying he would be "both investing [as well as] committing his time and extensive expertise" following his arrival.

However, the Blues announced his exit , external with a statement headlined 'Tom Brady departure'.

They added: "Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.

"It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community."

Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Following the end of his playing career, he acquired a stake in the Las Vegas Raiders while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.

On top of that, Brady's commitments include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

M John Harrison was billed by Booker bosses as "a genuinely original thinker"

Author M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.

Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.

The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.

Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."

Harrison (far left) with his fellow nominees (left-right) Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard, Rebecca Perry, Marlon James and Douglas Stuart

Dame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."

Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.

While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world".

"He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said.

"Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."

Listen back to a special edition of BBC Radio 4 Front Row from the Booker Prize ceremony

The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.

The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.

He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."

He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."

That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said , external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said , external : "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."

The Literary Review described it as , external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said , external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".

Another Telegraph critic wrote , external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books.

"And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday, Harrison explained how he had "wanted to write a book which really satirised the present-day barrage of information that we all suffer, without the necessary tools to understand what we're hearing and to analyse it and to have critical thinking about it".

He continued: "So the whole idea was to build a disaster in which it was a disaster of explanation, a disaster of the failure to understand the world as it was now. "

The Booker Prize is an annual award for the best novel written in the English language and published in the year up to 30 September. It was launched in 1969.

This year's other shortlisted books were:

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

When the shortlist was announced in September, Dame Mary said agreeing on the final six had been, "to put it mildly, hard work".

Another judge, US novelist Patricia Lockwood, said she had been "tossing books across the room" during judging sessions, while poet Raymond Antrobus described the selection as "a tussle".

The other judges were Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, and journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu.

Speaking about the final judging session, Dame Mary told reporters on Monday: "There was a lot of discussion, disagreement and debate. But nobody stomped off."

In a statement, she said the panel "spent a whole day debating the six remarkable novels on this year's shortlist" before reaching a unanimous decision to name Harrison the winner.

Jensen Huang, 63, has been called the 'Taylor Swift of tech' in the US

The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.

Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.

Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.

Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

Robinson's legal team is trying to get the death penalty taken off the table in his trial

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".

Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."

During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

The BBC's Ione Wells on how the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart

A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.

The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.

Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.

The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.

The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.

In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.

The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.

"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."

Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.

He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".

The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.

The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.

Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her so he would not be 'eaten up inside forever'

Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight

Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.

After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.

The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.

In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.

Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.

Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection - but says he would make the same decision again.

White, who has been named in Thomas Tuchel's squad for upcoming Nations League fixtures, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons.

Asked by BBC Radio 5 live's football correspondent John Murray what he would say to people who define his England career by what happened in Qatar, White said: "I think obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

"It's been amazing [though], obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it is amazing to be here now."

White is now 29 and asked if he would have done anything differently in hindsight, he added: "No, I don't think I would.

"Obviously, I was a bit younger, I am a bit older now.

"I think as a person I am quite real and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make.

"So, one that I am not happy about, but obviously it happened and [it is] time to move on."

White came on for his first England appearance since 2022 in March's 1-1 draw with Uruguay and was booed by some supporters before he scored but also gave away the penalty that led to the visitors' equaliser.

After that, Chelsea midfielder Jordan Henderson said he and his fellow England players would always support White, while Tuchel said recently that the defender deserves "a new chapter" and "positive feedback from the crowd".

Asked how he dealt with the emotions of that night at Wembley, White added: "Before the game I was thinking 'don't not stand out, but [take it] nice and easy'.

"So, it was obviously full of emotions that night, [but] it was a good night."

Kashim Chowdhury fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money

Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023.

He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work.

At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked.

She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial.

She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court.

Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.

That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.

In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.

Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.

But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs for several more months.

It was the government's National Fraud Initiative that flagged suspected fraud to Defra. As a result, the Defra Investigations Team launched an investigation and Chowdhury was arrested and interviewed under caution in July 2023. He was dismissed by the civil service in September 2023.

On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".

Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.

He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.

He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box.

Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.

He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".

But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system.

Chowdhury sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box

However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?

Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.

Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said.

"That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."

There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.

Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.

But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.

In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.

While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.

His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.

Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.

Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.

But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.

In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.

A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.

An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.

"Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said.

"But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."

A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions.

"This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."

The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers".

Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.

He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.

Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.

The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months.

Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.

At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.

Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

Watch: Moment Thomas Massie introduces articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth

A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record.

"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."

He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.

Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections.

He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."

Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January.

Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that".

He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject.

President Trump has indicated that he plans to stick by Hegseth , praising his leadership in the US capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year and defending his work during the war in Iran.

"We've made the world a lot safer place. Why haven't we gone after all these other people that ran wars and lost?" Trump said on Monday at the White House.

He also touted recruitment numbers under Hegseth.

"The soldiers, the actual soldiers, the great people that do the work, the great patriots, they love Pete Hegseth," he said. "He's done a very good job."

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office.

Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.

As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.

The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.

While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago.

He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years.

Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority.

Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins.

"There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.

Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.

While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term.

When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 67 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.

While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.

"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.

Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.

A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.

Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.

He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.

By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."

The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

A fire broke out at the factory following the explosion which some eyewitnesses confused with an earthquake

At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17.

Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.

At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.

The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

Michael Carrick has won 15 out of 32 games since taking over from Ruben Amorim as Manchester United's head coach in January

Manchester United's board is yet to make a final decision on Michael Carrick's future.

The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

The draw was Carrick's third match in charge since the board decided to give the 45-year-old more time to improve the side's form after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October.

The board felt Carrick - and the players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around, while the hierarchy were also aware that November's two-week break would offer an opportunity to reassess the situation in a calmer manner.

They are determined to do exactly that, knowing the results - one win, one draw and one defeat - and performances United have delivered in the past three games offer a mixed view of Carrick's tenure.

Conceding eight goals, winning only once and dropping into the relegation zone are obvious negatives. However, it is also felt fighting back from two goals down three times over the past two games showed that the players remain behind Carrick.

United's heirachy explored the possibility of replacing Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth last month, with ex-Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann considered.

Carrick said after the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa that he would not step down, but chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will be influential in the decision whether to keep the former Middlesbrough boss.

United travel to arch rivals Liverpool on 22 November in their first match after the international break, with Carrick's side in 18th place in the Premier League.

With just one league win so far this term, it is United's lowest position having played 10 matches since the 1986-87 campaign.

Following the Anfield trip, five of United's next seven league opponents are in the bottom half of the league. This includes the four other sides currently in the bottom five, with meetings against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland, all at Old Trafford.

Whether Carrick keeps his job or not, United will continue to struggle unless they stop conceding goals with such regularity.

Only Crystal Palace and Ipswich have let in more than United's 19 league goals.

They have conceded 15 times in the past three matches in all competitions. Their only clean sheet this term came against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK in the Champions League.

"All the Premier League teams, whether they play home or away against Manchester United, fancy their chances because you can open them up and score goals," former United assistant boss Rene Meulensteen told BBC Radio Five Live.

"No matter what combination you find it's just not good enough. I think Michael Carrick will be constantly puzzled as to what back four he can play because there's no certainty they can keep a clean sheet."

Full-back Diogo Dalot took the brunt of fan ire at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Huge cheers greeted his number being shown to confirm he was being replaced, which then turned to boos when he reached the dugout.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee, who suffered similar treatment when he was replaced after half an hour of a home defeat to Newcastle in December 2024, made a point of hugging Dalot as he made his way back to the bench.

Asked if it was time to take Dalot out of the firing line, Carrick urged caution.

"We've got to be careful with that," he said.

"I understand the frustration and I understand the disappointment of the supporters, I get it. We're all frustrated, we're all disappointed, and the players are as much as anyone, I guarantee you that.

"Diogo gives absolutely everything. He's played in different positions and played really well at times.

"He gives a penalty away. He knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better. He made a mistake. But I like what he brings to the team. He cares an awful lot and he's giving everything."

KIGALI — More than three decades after fleeing Rwanda at the end of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, Jean Léonard Teganya has been returned to the country, where he is wanted in connection with alleged genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Butare, Southern Rwanda.

The National Public Prosecution Authority said on November 9, 2026 that it had received Teganya following his deportation from the United States.

The plane carrying him touched down at Kigali International Airport around 6pm local time. It had initially been scheduled to arrive around 11am local time.

Teganya was indicted by Rwanda’s prosecution authority in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocide crimes committed in Butare, now part of Huye District in Southern Province.

His return closes one chapter of a long international case that took him from Rwanda to several countries, including Canada and the United States.

Teganya is now back in Rwanda, where prosecutors say he will face the judicial process over crimes allegedly committed during the 1994 genocide.

Teganya was born in 1971 in Gatumba Sector, in present-day Ngororero District, Western Province.

In 1994, he was studying medicine at the National University of Rwanda in Butare, now the University of Rwanda’s Huye campus. He was also an intern at the University Hospital of Butare.

According to evidence presented during his later trial in the United States, Teganya was also a member of the MRND, the political party that dominated the government before and during the genocide.

He was described as having been involved in the Interahamwe, the youth wing of the MRND.

The U.S. government said he participated in martial arts and weapons training through the group.

When the genocide against the Tutsi began on April 7, 1994, Teganya remained at the hospital in Butare.

U.S. prosecutors presented evidence that he led soldiers and Interahamwe members around the hospital looking for Tutsi patients and refugees who were hiding there.

According to the evidence presented at his 2019 trial, people who were found were taken away and killed behind the maternity ward.

Prosecutors also said Teganya led groups that took Tutsi women from the hospital to be raped.

The evidence presented in the U.S. case linked him to the killing of three Tutsi people at the hospital and four Tutsi students whom he found in the dormitory where he lived.

It also linked him to five rapes involving two Tutsi women hiding at the hospital.

These allegations formed the background to a U.S. immigration case that would eventually lead to his imprisonment.

Jean Leonard Teganya, a Rwandan man who U.S. prosecutors said participated in the African nation’s 1994 genocide and who was convicted in April of lying in hope of gaining asylum in the United States, is seen in this undated photo provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts, U.S., July 1, 2019. Courtesy U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts/Handout via REUTERS

As the genocide ended in July 1994, Teganya fled Rwanda.

His journey did not end in a neighbouring country.

According to the record of his U.S. appeal, Teganya left Rwanda for what was then Zaire and later travelled through Kenya and India. In 1999, he obtained a fake Zimbabwean passport and travelled to Canada.

Canada became the next major chapter in his attempt to remain outside Rwanda.

Teganya applied for asylum there in 1999.

Canadian authorities rejected his claim.

According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Canadian authorities determined twice that he was not entitled to asylum because of his alleged involvement in atrocities at the Butare hospital during the genocide.

His Canadian case continued for about 15 years.

Eventually, he was ordered to leave Canada.

Instead of complying, he remained there.

He would later cross another international border.

On August 3, 2014, Teganya was encountered walking after crossing the border from Canada into Houlton, Maine.

He then applied for asylum in the United States.

That application became the basis for the criminal case that would eventually send him to prison.

U.S. authorities said Teganya failed to disclose his membership in the MRND and his activities during the genocide.

He also made false statements during immigration proceedings about his past.

In 2017, federal prosecutors in Massachusetts charged him with immigration fraud and perjury.

The case attracted particular attention because the allegations concerned the use of the American asylum system by someone accused of participating in the very violence from which the system is designed to protect victims.

The U.S. government argued that Teganya had concealed his past to obtain immigration protection.

In April 2019, a federal jury convicted him on five counts — two counts of immigration fraud and three counts of perjury.

Teganya testified in his own defence and denied the extent of his involvement.

The U.S. First Circuit Court of Appeals later affirmed his convictions and sentence.

In its 2021 decision, the appeals court said the convictions were based on his failure to disclose his role in the Rwandan genocide to U.S. immigration authorities.

The court also noted that the trial had focused on the extent of his involvement in the genocide and that witnesses had testified about multiple murders, rapes and other atrocities involving Tutsi victims.

On July 1, 2019, U.S. District Judge F. Denis Saylor IV sentenced Teganya to 97 months in prison.

The judge also found that Teganya had obstructed justice by committing perjury during his trial.

The sentence was imposed for the immigration fraud and perjury convictions.

It was not a genocide conviction in the United States.

The U.S. case established criminal liability for lying to immigration authorities and for perjury. The allegations about his conduct during the genocide were central to the case and were presented as evidence explaining why he had concealed his past.

After completing his sentence, Teganya was expected to face removal proceedings.

The U.S. government had made clear that his imprisonment would not necessarily end his legal troubles.

While the United States prosecuted Teganya for immigration-related offences, Rwanda had its own case against him.

The National Public Prosecution Authority said it indicted him in 2014 for alleged genocide and crimes against humanity.

The alleged crimes were committed in Butare, the prosecution authority said.

That case remained significant because Teganya had never been tried in Rwanda for the genocide allegations described by prosecutors.

His return therefore brings him back to the jurisdiction where the alleged crimes occurred.

The precise next steps will be determined by Rwanda’s judicial authorities.

The prosecution authority has not, in the November 9 statement, announced the charges that will formally be presented in court following his deportation.

Teganya’s history illustrates how cases involving suspected genocide perpetrators can remain active for decades and cross several legal systems.

Canada rejected his asylum claim and ordered him removed.

The United States arrested and prosecuted him after he crossed the border from Canada.

The U.S. criminal case focused on his alleged concealment of his genocide history in his immigration applications.

The National Public Prosecution Authority expressed appreciation to U.S. judicial authorities for their cooperation in the deportation of genocide fugitives.

It also thanked the United States for continued cooperation on mutual legal assistance and for its contribution to international efforts to combat impunity and ensure accountability for genocide crimes.

That cooperation is important because many suspects in the 1994 genocide left Rwanda after the killings and established lives in other countries.

Some were granted refugee or immigration status before their alleged pasts became known.

Others have faced criminal or immigration proceedings years later.

The U.S. government has described Teganya’s case as part of a wider effort to prevent the country from becoming a safe haven for people accused of genocide, war crimes and other serious human rights abuses.

Its Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center was created in 2003 to help identify, investigate, prosecute and remove suspected human rights violators living in the United States.

The centre has worked with U.S. immigration and law-enforcement agencies on cases involving genocide, torture, ethnic cleansing and other forms of persecution.

In Teganya’s case, U.S. authorities worked with several agencies and international partners, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the State Department.

The U.S. Department of Justice has repeatedly described the case as an example of the importance of preventing people accused of atrocities from using immigration systems to obtain protection.

The National Public Prosecution Authority confirmed his arrival in Kigali this Monday evening November 9, 2026.

The authority has not yet detailed when he will appear before a court or the precise procedural steps that will follow.

What is clear is that the man who left Rwanda in the final days of the genocide has returned after more than 30 years outside the country.

His journey took him from a medical school in Butare to exile, Canada and the United States.

It included a rejected asylum claim, an illegal border crossing, a federal trial and a prison sentence.

But the U.S. case was never the final word on the genocide allegations against him.

Now, with Teganya back in the country, that case moves into a new phase.

For the survivors and families of those killed in Butare, his return represents another step in a long-running effort to bring suspected perpetrators before a court.

And for Rwanda’s justice system, it is the latest test of a principle that has defined its pursuit of genocide fugitives for more than three decades: that crossing a border does not erase responsibility for crimes committed during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.
